39754-franz-liszt:
James Huneker wrote this life of Franz Liszt, the great pianist and composer, published at New York in 1911. Huneker splits his subject into the real man and the legend, then turns to Liszt's art and character. A full chapter treats the B-minor Sonata and other piano pieces. Rome, Weimar, and Budapest, the three poles of Liszt's later life, get their own section.

Later chapters weigh Liszt as a composer, show him through the eyes of his peers, and trace his pupils. Pictures show his birthplace, his parents, his children, and Liszt at the piano. Huneker was a lively critic who knew the piano world well. His book reads as both biography and love letter to the instrument.
68522-life-of-liszt:
Louis Nohl wrote this Life of Liszt, translated from the German by George Upton and printed at Chicago in a sixth edition of 1902. It belongs to a cheap series of musicians' lives: Mozart, Beethoven, Haydn, and Wagner at seventy five cents each, with portraits. A portrait of Franz Liszt fronts the book.

The translator's preface warns that the little work is rather an essay on Liszt's personal and musical character than a biography. Nohl wrote with strong admiration and affection for his hero, unlike most of his other subjects. The testimony of all who knew Liszt, he adds, praises the man's charm. The book sketches the virtuoso who reinvented the piano recital and the abbé he became, for American parlor readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-liszt:
Franz Liszt, admittedly the greatest pianist in music's annals, was born at Raiding in Hungary on 22 October 1811 and died at Bayreuth on 31 July 1886. He was a composer whose standing still divides critics. His precocity was recognised early. His father Adam Liszt, a musical amateur of rare taste, taught him first, and his debut at Oedenburg at nine so startled Hungarian magnates that they funded his further education. Taken to Vienna, he studied piano six years with Czerny and theory with Salieri and Randhartinger.

 Brilliant concert tours followed. In later years he turned to sacred music, oratorios, and teaching at Weimar, Rome, and Budapest, shaping generations of pianists. His own compositions, from symphonic poems to psalm settings, remained debated masterpieces.
